1. Heard. Leave Granted.
2. On 20.10.2024, acting on secret information that a
person was selling narcotic substances near Arumbakkam
Naduvankarai  Bridge,  Chennai,  the  police  intercepted
Arunkumar (A1) and allegedly recovered 11.59 grams of
methamphetamine from him. According to the prosecution,
his statement disclosed that he purchased the substance
from Anthony Ruban (A4) for onward sale to other accused.
1

## Page 34

A  further  quantity  was  allegedly  recovered  from  his
residence.  Subsequent  arrests  and  statements  of  other
accused led the police to the Appellant, Vishwanathan @
Makunda Vishwanatha Reddy, from whom one kilogram of
methamphetamine was allegedly seized. The prosecution
alleged  that  a  principal  supplier,  A15,  procured  the
contraband from Delhi and supplied it to the Appellant and
others. T wenty persons were implicated in Crime No. 441 of
2024 registered at K8 Arumbakkam Police Station.
3. The Appellant was arrested and remanded to judicial
custody  on  23.10.2024.  Following  completion  of  the
investigation, the final report was filed in C.C. No.643 of
2025 before the II Additional Special Court for Exclusive
Trial of Cases under the  Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic
Substances Act, 1985 (“NDPS”) at  Chennai. The offences
invoked included Sections 8(c), 22(b), 29(1), 25 and 20(b)
(ii)(A) of the NDPS Act. The Appellant denied involvement,
contending  that  he  had  been  implicated  through
statements of co-accused and that the alleged recovery
was affected by procedural irregularities, including a delay
2

## Page 35

of 34 days in producing the seized substance before the
court. He also relied on the grant of bail to several co-
accused.
4. During his incarceration, the Appellant stated that he
suffered a cardiac event on 04.04.2025 and was admitted
to Stanley Government Hospital, Chennai, where Coronary
Artery  Bypass  Grafting  (CABG)  was  advised.  His  wife,
Suneetha,  subsequently  approached  the  High  Court
seeking permission for treatment at a private hospital. By
order  dated  11.08.2025,  the  High  Court  directed  the
authorities  to  consider  her  representation  dated
17.07.2025 and pass appropriate orders within one week.
Meanwhile,  the  Appellant’s  earlier  bail  application  was
dismissed  on  21.03.2025,  and  another  application  was
dismissed as withdrawn on 05.11.2025.
5. By the impugned order dated 26.02.2026, the Madras
High Court dismissed the Appellant’s third bail application,
Crl. O.P . No. 33219 of 2025. It found that the arrest memo
contained  the  grounds  of  arrest,  that  the  inventory
3

## Page 36

proceedings had been conducted before a Magistrate, and
that  the  alleged  delay  in  sending  samples  for  forensic
examination did not, by itself, justify bail. Considering the
alleged  recovery  of  commercial  quantity  and  the
Appellant’s failure to satisfy the conditions under Section
37 of the NDPS Act, the High Court declined relief. The
Appellant challenged that order in the present Appeal.
6. The  Appellant  submitted  that  he  had  been  falsely
implicated solely on the basis of statements of co-accused,
that his name did not appear in the FIR, and that there was
no  legally  admissible  evidence  connecting  him  with  the
alleged offence. He contended that the grounds of arrest
had not been furnished to him and questioned compliance
with  the  mandatory  safeguards  under  the  NDPS  Act,
particularly the unexplained delay of 34 days in producing
the allegedly seized contraband before the court and the
delay  in  sending  it  for  forensic  examination.  He  further
submitted that the investigation was complete, the charge-
sheet had been filed, he had remained in custody since
23.10.2024,  and  several  co-accused  had  already  been
4

## Page 37

granted bail, entitling him to consideration on the ground
of  parity.  Additionally,  he  relied  on  his  serious  cardiac
condition,  stating  that  he  had  suffered  a  cardiac  event
while in custody and had been advised CABG, requiring
specialised  treatment  and  postoperative  care.  On  these
grounds,  he  sought  release  on  bail  and  undertook  to
comply with any conditions imposed by the Court.
7. On the other hand, the Counsel appearing for the
Respondent/Union of India vehemently opposed the bail of
the Appellant.
8. Having  heard  learned  counsel  for  the  parties  and
perused the material on record, we find that the appellant
has been in custody since 23.10.2024 for almost a period
of 2 years. Though the Chargesheet has been filed, the trial
is yet to commence.
9. The appellant having been arrested on the basis of
statements made by the co-accused, the admissibility and
evidentiary value of those statements are matters to be
examined  by  the  trial  court  upon  appreciation  of  the
5

## Page 38

evidence adduced by the parties.
10. Having regard to the fact that the charge-sheet cites
46 prosecution witnesses and the trial is yet to commence,
and  considering  that  the  veracity  of  the  disclosure
statement  on  the  basis  of  which  the  appellant  was
arrested, as well as his alleged involvement in the offence,
requires examination during trial, we are of the opinion that
his continued incarceration, after having undergone almost
two years in custody, is not warranted. Accordingly, the
appellant deserves to be enlarged on bail.
11. We  make  it  clear  that,  we  have  refrained  from
expressing any opinion on the merits of these contentions.
All  questions  concerning  the  appellant’s  alleged
involvement, the reliability of the prosecution evidence and
compliance with the statutory safeguards are left open for
determination by the trial court in accordance with law.
12. Having regard to the medical report received and the
past medical history of the appellant also persuade us to
enlarge the appellant on bail. For the aforesaid reasons, the
6

## Page 39

appeal  is  allowed,  and  the  appellant  is  directed  to  be
enlarged  on  bail  on  such  terms  and  conditions  as  the
jurisdictional court may deem fit to impose.
13. Pending application(s), if any, stands consigned to
records.

1. Leave granted. 
2. The present appeal arises from the judgment and order 
dated 13.05.2025 passed by the Gauhati High Court, 
Kohima Bench (hereinafter referred to as the “High 
Court”) in Criminal Petition No. 32 of 2022, whereby 
the High Court dismissed the petition filed by the 
appellant under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal 
Procedure, 1973 (hereinafter referred to as the “CrPC”), 
seeking quashing of C.R. Case No. 17 of 2022 pending 
before the Court of the Judicial Magistrate First Class, 
Dimapur, Nagaland, for offences p unishable under 
Sections 417 and 420 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 
(hereinafter referred to as the “IPC”). 
3. The facts giving rise to the present appeal are as 
follows: 

## Page 43

Crl.A.@ SLP(Crl.)No.10621 of 2025  2 
 
3.1. The appellant was serving as the Chief Executive 
Officer of Darjeeling Organic Tea Estates Private 
Limited (hereinafter referred to as the “Company”) 
and was authorised to act on its behalf. Respondent 
No. 1, who is the proprietor of C.R. Traders, entered 
into negotiations with the Company in relation to the 
Jamguri Tea Estate situated at Golaghat , Assam. 
Prior to the execution of the agreement, respondent 
No. 1 addressed a communication dated 31.05.2021 
to UCO Bank in relation to the Tea Estate and its 
mortgage with the Bank. 
3.2. A Memorandum of Understanding dated 01.06.2021 
(hereinafter referred to as the “MoU”) was thereafter 
executed between the Company and C.R. Traders. 
The appellant signed the MoU on behalf of the 
Company in his capacity as its authorised signatory. 
Pursuant thereto, respondent No. 1 transferred an 
amount of Rs. 40,00,000/- (Rupees Forty Lakh only) 
to the bank account of the Company on 07.06.2021 
in two transactions of Rs. 39,95,000/ - (Rupees 
Thirty-Nine Lakh Ninety -Five Thousand only) and  
Rs. 5,000/- (Rupees Five Thousand only). 
3.3. Disputes subsequently arose between the parties 
regarding performance of the obligations under the 
MoU. The MoU was terminated by a communication 

## Page 44

Crl.A.@ SLP(Crl.)No.10621 of 2025  3 
 
dated 26.07.2021 on the ground that respondent No. 
1 had failed to comply with its terms and conditions. 
3.4. On 17.08.2022, respondent No. 1 instituted a 
criminal complaint against the appellant before the 
Judicial Magistrate First Class, Dimapur, Nagaland. 
It was alleged that the appellant had induced 
respondent No. 1 to part with the amount of Rs. 
40,00,000/- (Rupees Forty Lakh only) by 
representing that the Jamguri Tea Estate belonged 
to the Company, whereas it was owned by Bhumya  
Tea Company Private Limited and was the subject 
matter of proceedings involving UCO Bank. On the 
basis of these allegations, offences punishable under 
Sections 417 and 420 of IPC were alleged against the 
appellant. The complaint came to be registered as 
C.R. Case No. 17 of 2022. 
3.5. By order dated 21.09.2022, the Judicial Magistrate 
First Class, Dimapur, found prima facie grounds to 
proceed against the appellant for offences 
punishable under Sections 417 and 420 IPC and 
issued summons to him. 
3.6. The appellant thereafter approached the High Court 
under Section 482 of CrPC seeking quashing of the 
criminal proceedings. He contended, inter alia, that 
the dispute arose out of a purely contractual 

## Page 45

Crl.A.@ SLP(Crl.)No.10621 of 2025  4 
 
transaction, that the MoU had been entered into by 
the Company and not by him in his personal 
capacity, that the amount of Rs. 40,00,000/ - 
(Rupees Forty Lakh only) had been transferred to the 
account of the Company, and that the Company 
itself had not been arrayed as an accused. 
3.7. By the impugned judgment dated 13.05.2025, the 
High Court dismissed the petition upon holding that 
a prima facie case under Sections 417 and 420 IPC 
was made out and that the existence of an 
arbitration clause in the MoU did not furnish a 
ground for quashi ng the criminal proceedings. 
Aggrieved thereby, the appellant is before us. 
4. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment, the 
appellant has preferred the present appeal. 
5. We have heard learned counsel for the parties and have 
carefully perused the material placed on record. 
6. The distinction between a breach of contract and the 
offence of cheating is well settled. For an offence under 
Sections 417 and 420 of IPC, the fraudulent or 
dishonest intention must exist at the inception of the 
transaction and must have induced the complainant to 
part with property. A subsequent failure to perform  a 
contractual obligation cannot, by itself, give rise to an 
inference of such intention. Recently, in G. 

## Page 46

Crl.A.@ SLP(Crl.)No.10621 of 2025  5 
 
Saminathan and Another v. State, represented by 
the Sub-Inspector of Police and Another (2026 INSC 
772), this Court reiterated that for establishing the 
offence of cheating, the complainant must show 
fraudulent or dishonest intention at the time when the 
promise or representation was made. 
7. Tested on the above principles, the complaint does not 
disclose the necessary ingredients of cheating against 
the appellant. The MoU was entered into between 
respondent No. 1 and the Company. The appellant 
signed it only in his capacity as the Chief Execut ive 
Officer and authorised signatory of the Company. More 
importantly, the amount of Rs. 40,00,000/ - (Rupees 
Forty Lakh only) was transferred directly to the account 
of the Company and there is no allegation that the 
appellant received or appropriated any part thereof for 
his personal benefit. 
8. The principal allegation of respondent No. 1 is that the 
appellant induced her to part with the amount by 
falsely representing that the Jamguri  Tea Estate 
belonged to the Company. The complaint states that 
the appellant was “well aware of the fact that the said 
Jamguri Tea Estate and Tea Factory... does not belong 
to the company” and nevertheless made a false 
representation. However, this asserti on of dishonest 

## Page 47

Crl.A.@ SLP(Crl.)No.10621 of 2025  6 
 
intention has to be considered in the context of the 
transaction as a whole . Even prior to execution of the 
MoU, respondent No. 1 was aware that the Tea Estate 
was mortgaged with UCO Bank. The MoU itself 
contemplated the clearance of the outstanding dues 
and encumbrances of UCO Bank and the eventual 
acquisition of the Tea Estate.  The material on record 
further indicates that the Company was in possession 
of and operating the Tea Estate and had substantial 
claims concerning the same. In these circumstances, a 
bare assertion that the appellant knew the 
representation to be false doe s not, without more, 
establish dishonest intention at the inception of the 
transaction. 
9. The subsequent events also bear the character of a 
contractual dispute. Differences arose regarding 
performance of the reciprocal obligations under the 
MoU, which was ultimately terminated on 26.07.2021. 
Whether such termination was valid and whether 
respondent No. 1 is entitled to refund of the amount 
paid or any other relief are matters carrying civil 
consequences. They cannot assume a criminal 
character merely because the contractual relationship 
subsequently failed. 

## Page 48

Crl.A.@ SLP(Crl.)No.10621 of 2025  7 
 
10. The High Court was correct in observing that the 
existence of an arbitration clause does not, by itself, bar 
criminal proceedings. That proposition, however, does 
not answer the real question. The Court must first 
determine whether the allegations disclose  the 
essential ingredients of the criminal offence alleged. In 
the present case, the material does not disclose 
sufficient factual foundation to infer that the appellant, 
at the inception of the transaction, acted with the 
dishonest intention necessary to constitute cheating. 
11. We are, therefore, of the considered view that 
continuation of the criminal proceedings against the 
appellant would amount to giving a predominantly 
contractual dispute the colour of a criminal 
prosecution. The ingredients of the offences under 
Sections 417 and 420 IPC are not made out against the 
appellant and continuation of the proceedings would 
amount to an abuse of the process of law. 
12. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed. The impugned 
judgment and order dated 13.05.2025 passed by the 
High Court in Criminal Petition No. 32 of 2022 is set 
aside. 
13. Consequently, C.R. Case No. 17 of 2022 pending 
before the Court of the Judicial Magistrate First Class, 
Dimapur, Nagaland, along with all proceedings arising 

## Page 49

Crl.A.@ SLP(Crl.)No.10621 of 2025  8 
 
therefrom, stands quashed insofar as the appellant is 
concerned. It is clarified that this order shall not 
preclude respondent No. 1 from pursuing any remedy 
available in law in respect of her civil or contractual 
claims. 
14. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

2. The appeal is filed by a grieving father against the 
order of the High Court quashing the cognizance taken under 
Sections 302 and 201 of Indian Penal Code 1 against the 2 nd 
respondent-accused; in an incident where the appellant’s son 
drowned to death. 
3. We heard  learned Counsel for the appellant , 
respondent-State and the 2nd respondent. 
4. Learned Counsel for the 2nd respondent, at the outset , 
submitted that there was  cognizance taken by the Judicial 
Magistrate First Class, IV, Darbhanga and hence , this appeal

5. We notice, on the facts of th is case, that the appellant 
was the first informant who spoke of the deceased having been

near the State Boring and that despite his best effort s to save

had disappeared having been swept away in the currents. This 
was the First Information Statement leading to the FIR, as seen 
from Annexure P1.

6. The Police conducted the investigation and filed a final

directed the protest petition  filed to be numbered as 
complaint by order dated 29.10.2021 and posted the

who was directed to be present.  
7. A revision was taken from the order of the Judicial

cognizance in the case. The l earned Magistrate , on re -
examination of the materials, took cognizance, which has now 
been set at naught by the High Court; according to us, in a very 
casual manner, totally ignoring the compelling circumstances 
as has been brought out in the revision al order of the 7 th 
Additional Sessions Judge. 
8. On the consequence of a final report filed by the Police, 
which is termed a ‘closure report ’, we extract  herein 
paragraph 16 of Brajesh Kumar alias Birjesh Kumar Singh v. 

## Page 54

Page 4 of 8 
 
 
State of Bihar2, (authored by one of us, K. Vinod Chandran, J.) 
:-  
‘16. Ram Naresh Prasad v. State of Jharkhand (2009) 11 SCC 299 
held that when the police file a report, colloquially termed 
a ‘closure report’; finding no sustainable case made out, 
the Court cannot direct a charge sheet to be filed, but 
could always take cognizance on the basis of the material 
in the report or direc t further investigation. H.S. Bains v. 
State (U.T. of Chandigarh) (1980) 4 SCC 631 & Ramswaroop Soni 
v. State of M.P. (2020) 18 SCC 327 reiterated that when a closure 
report is filed finding no offence made out, the Court has 
three options; (i ) to accept the same and close the 
proceedings or (ii) take cognizance of the matter on the 
materials in the report or (iii) direct further investigation. 
It is thus open to the Magistrate on submission of a closure 
report to look into the material facts disclosed in the report 
and form an opinion as to whether it constitutes an offence 
and take cognizance of the offence under Section 
190(1)(b). To buttress this position, Abhinandan Jha1967 SCC 
OnLine SC 107  made reference to Section 169 of the Code 
which provides that even if the police officer finds on 
investigation that there is no reasonable ground or 
sufficient evidence to put the accused on trial, the officer 
while releasing the accused has to take a bo nd for 
appearance before the Magistrate, if required. The 
primacy of the Court to take cognizance or deny it is the 
law discernible from the very provisions of the CrPC.’ 
 
9. With the above principle in mind, we look at the 
impugned order of the learned Single Judge. The impugned 
order first found that the postmortem did not suggest anything 
sinister, since the ‘death was due to asphyxia and ventricular 
fibrillation as a result of drowning in water ’. We are afraid that 
the assumption is wrong, insofar as even if a person is pushed

into the water deliberately with the intention of drowning him,

indicated death by drowning, it cannot be assumed that there 
was absolutely no foul play, since the specific contention taken 
up was that the deceased was taken by the 2nd respondent, and 
a little later, he was found drowning and there were attempts 
by third parties to save him. There were two witnesses who  
also spoke of having seen the 2nd respondent fleeing from the 
scene of occurrence; which makes it sinister and a trial , 
expedient to unravel the mystery regarding the death . 
Especially when the 2 nd respondent who took the deceased 
from his house, with whom he was last seen, should proffer an 
explanation, more so, when he was found running away from 
the spot.  
10. The further reasoning in the impugned judgment is that 
the FIR was lodged after the father of the deceased received 
information of the drowning of his son, which information was 
not disclosed in the FIR. A reading of the FIR , produced as 
Annexure P1, clearly indicates that the information was passed 
on to the father through one Ashok Chaudhary, who informed

the family members of the appellant. On such information 
having been received, he rushed to the spot and arranged

appellant’s doorsteps, and a little later , Ashok Chaudhary 
having informed the drowning of his son. The finding of the 
High Court is flawed insofar as the documents having not been

11. We also find that the High Court has not looked at the

trial. The decision s with respect to cognizance despite a

the impugned judgment deserves to be set aside.

prayer clause (a).
b) The Respondent is directed to either furnish a
bank guarantee issued by a Nationalized Bank or a
Scheduled Commercial Bank for the Appellant's
claim of USD 66,92,500 along with interest and
costs or its INR equivalent to the satisfaction
of the Prothonotary and Senior Master of this
Court, within a period of 2 weeks from the date
of this order;

if unable to comply with the above directions the
Respondent is restrained from the alienating or
creating third party rights, title or interest
with respect to the subject property mentioned in
prayer  clause  (d)  till  completion  of  the
arbitration proceedings.”

correctness of the judgment/order of the learned Single Judge
dated 08.01.2026 dismissing the petition/application under

Non-Reportable
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal No.18067 of 2017
Principal Officer LG Electronics
India Pvt. Ltd Thr. Its Authorized
Signatory Mr. Ashish Agrawal
...Appellant
Versus
Assistant Commissioner of
Income Tax, NOIDA and Anr.     
 ...Respondents
W I T H
Civil Appeal No.18068 of 2017
A N D
Civil Appeal No.18281 of 2017
O R D E R
The appellant/assessee under the Income Tax Act, 1961 1 was
concerned with the notice issued under Sections 147/148 of the Act;
which the High Court refused to interfere with and hence the appeal.
2. Essentially the reassessment was proposed for the Assessment
Years 2006-07, 2007-08 and 2008-09 alleging that parent company
of the assessee, M/s L.G. Electronics Korea and other associated
enterprises were running a Permanent Establishment (PE) in India,
thereby obligating the assessee to deduct TDS on the remittances
made to the parent company and the associated enterprises. The
notices  under  Section  148  for  the  relevant  years  are  dated
1  For brevity, “the IT Act”

## Page 77

28.03.2013, 21.03.2014 and 31.03.2015 produced in the respective
appeals as Annexures P11, P11 and P1.  It was alleged that income
of the assessee had escaped assessment, since the failure to deduct
TDS  brings  in  a  consequence  of  disallowance  of  such  expenses
under Section 40 (a) (i) of the IT Act. 
3. The  assessee  before  the  High  Court  urged  the  ground  of
limitation pointing out that there is nothing to show that income has
escaped assessment due to the failure on the part of the assessee
to disclose complete and full facts or that the assessee was guilty of
concealment of facts. The reassessment thus is reduced to a mere
change of opinion, which cannot be permitted. The Double Taxation
Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) between India and Korea was also put
forth along with the other grounds.
4. The Division Bench of the High Court found that proceedings
were taken against the Korean Company and it is related entities to
tax  the  chargeable  income  in  their  hands  and  there  were  also
proceedings initiated against the appellant company under Section
201 of the IT Act for recovery of amount of tax, not deducted at
source.  The  third  consequence,  which  arose  from  the  survey
conducted  under  Section  133A  of  the  IT  Act,  was  the  instant
proceedings to disallow the related expenses under Section 40(a)(i)
for failure to deduct taxes. The Division Bench left the question of
DTAA  to  be  considered  in  the  reassessment  proceedings  and

## Page 78

negatived  the  contention  of  limitation;  since,  there  was  no
disclosure  with  respect  to  the  Permanent  Establishment  of  the
Korean Company operating in India. The notice under Section 148
for initiating reassessment proceedings under Section 147 does not
call for any interference, held the impugned order.
5. Sri Deepak Chopra, Learned Senior Counsel for the assessee,
pointed  out that the reassessment proceedings were carried out
and, in an appeal, there was an order under Section 250 of IT Act
communicated, without anything written on the same and enclosing
in two blank papers. The assessee’s further appeal was frustrated,
and it is informed that the incumbent CIT (Appeals) NOIDA, who
issued the blank order, was later suspended. As of now, unless the
notice issued under  Section  148 is interfered with,  the assessee
would be left remediless.
6. Sri  Raghavendra  P.  Shankar,  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General,  on  the  other  hand,  pointed  out  that  the  parallel
proceedings initiated under Section 201 stand allowed in favour of
the assessee by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal (ITAT). What
remains is for the appellant to produce the said order either before
the  officer  who  conducted  the  reassessment  or  in  an  appeal
instituted,  which  could  be  reckoned  to  delete  the  disallowance
carried out on this ground. The learned ASG would contend that
since reassessment order is not produced, he is unable to assist as

## Page 79

to whether there were grounds on which reassessment was carried
out.
7. The order of the ITAT from the proceedings under Section 201
is  produced  as  Annexure  A1  in  I.A.  No.118536  of  2025  in  C.A.
No.18067 of 2017. From a reading of the order, we find that the
proceedings initiated under Section 201 were taken in appeal and on
the  directions  of  the  Dispute  Resolution  Panel  (DRP),  the  First
Appellate Authority modified the order, determining profits at 20%
markup on 50% salary cost of the expatriate employees, attributed
to the Permanent Establishment of L.G. Korea, in India. It was also
noticed that the assessment proceedings initiated against L.G. Korea
was quashed by the ITAT for non-implementation of the directions of
the DRP. The said appellate orders for the assessment years 2005-
06 to 2010-11 were not challenged, since it had low tax effect. The
ITAT, in the proceedings under Section 201, held that there is no tax
liability on the payee i.e. L.G. Korea and hence there is no obligation
on the assessee to withhold tax under Section 195 of the Act. The
appellant/assessee  was  found  not  liable  to  be  treated  as  an
‘assessee-in-default’ under Section 201 of the Act. If the assessee
cannot be treated as an ‘assessee-in-default’ under Section 201,
necessarily there can be any disallowance made under Section 40(a)
(i) of the IT Act and hence even if the reassessment proceedings
have been carried out, we are of the opinion that it requires no

## Page 80

remand to the Assessing Officer.
8. We also take note of the submission of ASG that there could be
other  grounds  on  which  reassessment  was  actually  carried  out,
which we cannot subscribe to. The notice under Section 147 was
only  with  respect  to  the  default  under  Section  201  and  the
disallowance of the expenses claimed under Section 40(a)(i) of the
Act. If the ground on which reassessment is found to be initiated is
untenable, then there is no question of any other ground coming
forth in the reassessment proceedings being utilized for the purpose
of determining escapement of income. We, hence, hold that the
reassessment  proceedings  initiated  are  unenforceable  for  the
assessment years 2006-07 to 2008-09.  The appellant shall produce
our decision and the decision of the ITAT produced as Annexure A1
under Section 201 proceedings before the Assessing Officer who
shall close the reassessment proceedings as unenforceable.
9. The appeals are allowed.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

5. Having regard to the nature of the proceedings and
the rate at which the progress of the trial has taken place,
we  are  unable  to  accept  the  contention  raised  by  the
learned counsel appearing for the respondent – State that
trial would be concluded within three months. Chargesheet
having been filed on completion of the investigation and
the prosecution would have to establish the guilt of the
accused  beyond  reasonable  doubt  on  the  basis  of  the
books, accounts etc., namely, the said material evidence,
we are of the considered view that continued incarceration
of the appellants is not warranted. Hence, the appeals are
allowed, impugned orders are set aside and appellants are
ordered to be released on regular bail on such terms and
conditions  as  the  jurisdictional  court  may  deem  fit  to
3

## Page 106

impose. 
6. Pending application(s), if any, stands consigned to
records.

Civil Appeals arising out of   SLP (CIVIL) No. 24740 of 2024, SLP  
(CIVIL) No. 1655 of 2025 and SLP (CIVIL) No. 27304 of 2024
1. Leave granted.
2. These three appeals are directed against an interlocutory
order dated 18.09.2024 passed by a Division Bench of the Gujarat
High Court in R/MCA No.366/2022 whereby the three appellants have
been ordered to be impleaded in the pending contempt proceedings.
3. Those contempt proceedings have been initiated at the instance
of the first respondent, who happens to be the husband of the
appellant in the first appeal (Civil Appeal arising out of SLP(C)
No.24740/2024). At the outset, it is worth noting that the first
respondent and the above-mentioned appellant are judicial officers
1

## Page 110

and  they  were  husband  and  wife  at  the  relevant  time.  The
unfortunate matrimonial dispute led to registration of an FIR at
the instance of the appellant (Priyanka Lal) and subsequently the
first respondent was arrested in that case. Alleging that the
arrest was made in flagrant violation of the mandatory guidelines
laid down by this Court in Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar and Anr.,
(2014) 8 SCC 273, the contempt proceedings were initially filed
against  the  police  officers/officials.  However,  the  first
respondent subsequently impleaded his wife; the appellant (another
judicial officer) in the appeal arising out of SLP (Civil) No.
27304/2024, as well as the Assistant Public Prosecutor, who is the
appellant in the appeal arising out of SLP (Civil) No. 1655/2025.
4. We  have  heard  learned  senior  counsel/counsel  for  the
appellants, the Respondent (Kshitijkumar Satishbhai Banker), as
well as Mr. K.M. Nataraj, learned Additional Solicitor General of
India, representing the High Court.
5. It is not in dispute that during the pendency of these
proceedings, the unfortunate matrimonial dispute has been amicably
resolved  between  the  appellant,  Priyanka  Lal,  and  the  first
respondent. Accordingly, we find no valid grounds to continue with
the contempt proceedings against the said appellant. Therefore, the
Civil Appeal arising from SLP(C) No.24740/2024 is hereby allowed,
and the summoning order against the appellant is quashed.
6. With regard to the second appeal submitted by M.I. Sheikh, the
Assistant Public Prosecutor, his sole involvement appears to be
that he was a neighbour of the appellant and is alleged to have
been a co-conspirator in the proceedings that resulted in the
2

## Page 111

respondent/contempt petitioner's arrest. In our considered opinion,
such a circumstance alone may not constitute sufficient ground to
initiate  contempt  proceedings  against  the  Assistant  Public
Prosecutor, particularly given that the appellant wife, who is the
alleged primary conspirator, has already been granted the requisite
relief. Therefore, Civil Appeal arising from SLP (Civil) No.
1655/2025 is hereby allowed, and the order summoning him in the
contempt proceedings is also set aside.
7. Finally, adverting to the third appeal preferred by A.M.
Bhukharee, a Judicial Officer, it is not disputed that he was
merely a neighbor of the appellant in the first case and has been
impleaded as a party in contempt proceedings based on certain
allegations. Since those allegations no longer persist against the
appellant wife, we find no valid ground to proceed against Mr. A.M.
Bhukharee. Consequently, the Civil Appeal arising out of SLP
(Civil) No. 27304/2024 is allowed, and the summons in the contempt
proceedings against him are also set aside.
8. For the reasons aforesaid, all three appeals stand allowed,
and the impugned order to the extent of summoning of the appellants
Priyanka Lal, M.I. Sheikh and A.M. Bhukharee is hereby quashed.
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 163 OF 2025
9. The instant writ petition is filed by the petitioner, a
Judicial Officer, who has been placed under suspension. The genesis
of the suspension order lies in an unfortunate matrimonial dispute
between the first petitioner and her husband, namely, Kshitij Kumar
Satishbhai Banker. In the separate proceedings we disposed of
3

## Page 112

today, we noted that the matrimonial dispute has since been
amicably resolved between the parties. That being so, it seems to
us that the order of suspension or any decision taken to initiate
disciplinary proceedings against the petitioner (Priyanka Lal and
A.M. Bhukharee) may be sympathetically reconsidered by the High
Court.
10.  We, therefore, dispose of this writ petition with a request to
the High Court to take notice of the subsequent circumstances and
take an appropriate decision as early as possible, and preferably
within four weeks.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.

contained in the Settlement Agreement dated 24.07.2026.
Accordingly, it is prayed that appropriate and necessary
orders may be passed in terms thereof.
3. The parties, who appear through video conferencing
mode, are duly identified by their respective learned
counsel, and have accepted and acknowledged the factum of
the Settlement Agreement dated 24.07.2026 having been
entered into between them.
4. We appreciate the efforts taken by Ms. Shalini Atri,
learned Mediator, Supreme Court Mediation Centre, who
1

## Page 116

mediated  the  dispute  between  the  parties.  We  also
appreciate  the  efforts  put  in  by  learned  counsel

“ 1. That the parties to the present agreement
have finally and mutually agreed and decided to
dissolve  their  marriage  by  seeking  an
appropriate  order  from  the  Hon'ble  Supreme
Court of India in Transfer Petition (Crl.) No.
783 of 2026.   
2. That the parties have mutually decided that
there shall be no amount payable by the Second
Party to the First Party. The Second Party has
returned all Stridhan/ gifts belonging to the
First Party and the First Party has received
all such Stridhan/ gifts. The First Party has
not raised any monetary demand to effectuate
the preset settlement terms.
3. That it is agreed between the parties that
the First Party will co-operate in signing the
documents/ affidavits required for quashing of
FIR bearing No. 450 / 2023, P.S. Alipur, Delhi,
Cr. Case 4660 of 2025 titled State v. Nitesh
Mishra  and  Ors  and  appear  before  Hon'ble
Supreme Court of India (and or any other Court)
as and when summoned / required by the Hon'ble
Court.
4.  That  it  is  further  agreed  between  the
parties that they will move a joint application
seeking an order for dissolution of marriage by
divorce before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of
India and any other Court (if required).
5. That both the parties assures that they will
withdraw all their complaints or court cases
filed anywhere in India against each other, if
any. It is further agreed that even otherwise
any such Complaint / Case lodged by either
party against the other shall be deemed to be
withdrawn or settled in view of the amicable
settlement between the parties.
2

## Page 117

6. That it is further agreed that after the
execution of the terms and conditions stated
above there shall be no claim left between the
parties against each other or their respective
parents or families in any manner whatsoever.
Both the parties shall not raise any claim or
right over the assets / property immovable or
movable of the other party or their parents and
relatives in future.
7. That it is further agreed that pursuant to
the issuance of decree of divorce the parties
to the agreement including their parents shall
not file or pursue any criminal, civil or other

8.  That  it  is  further  agreed  between  the

may defame or lower the reputation of the other

9. That both the parties undertake to abide by
the terms of the present settlement and the
terms of the present settlement are final and
binding on both the parties.
10. That both the parties have executed this

11.  That  this  agreement  constitutes  the

Leave granted.
2. The present appeal has been preferred challenging the final
judgement and order dated 29.05.2026, passed by the High Court
of Judicature at Allahabad in Criminal Appeal No. 902 of 1988.
3. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that the prosecution
case  was  set  in  motion  upon  receipt  of  a  written  application
lodged by the complainant at Police Station Didauli, Moradabad
on 12.08.1983. Pursuant thereto, FIR No. 185 of 1983 came to be
registered.  The  complainant  alleged  that  during  the  preceding
night, five to six unknown miscreants had entered his thatched
shed and kidnapped his ten year old son. On the basis of the said
1

## Page 122

allegations, Case Crime No. 218 of 1985 came to be registered
under  Section  364 of  the  Indian  Penal  Code,  1860  (for  short
“IPC”) against unknown persons. On 12.08.1983, the son of the
complainant was recovered from the custody of one of the co-
accused.
3.1 Upon completion of the investigation, the Police submitted
charge-sheets against the five accused persons, amongst whom,
one accused person was absconding and was not part in the
present  trial.  The  Trial  Court  framed  charges  against  the
appellant  and  two  other  co-accused  persons  named,
Harishchandra and Bholu for offences punishable under Section
147 and Section 364 read with Section 149 of the IPC. Charges
were framed against another co-accused person named, Dulha
under Section 368 of IPC. 
3.2 The Trial Court, vide its  judgement  dated 06.04.1988 in
Sessions Trial No. 70 of 1985, acquitted one of the co-accused
persons namely Bholu and convicted another co-accused person,
namely  Dulha  under  Section  368  of  IPC.  The  Trial  Court
convicted the appellant herein and another co-accused person,
2

## Page 123

named  Harishchandra  for  the  commission  of  an  offence
punishable under Section 364 read with Section 149 of the IPC
and sentenced them to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three
years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/-. The appellant and another
co-accused were further convicted under Section 147 of the IPC
and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years.
Both of the sentences were to run concurrently.
3.3 Aggrieved  by  the  judgement  of  conviction  and  order  of
sentence,  the  appellant  and  other  two  co-accused  persons
preferred Criminal Appeal No. 902 of 1988 before the High Court
of Judicature at Allahabad. By the impugned judgement dated
29.05.2026, the High Court dismissed the appeal affirming the
conviction and sentence.
3.4 Aggrieved by the dismissal of his appeal by the High Court,
the appellant has preferred the present appeal.
4. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and learned
special counsel for the respondent-State of Uttar Pradesh. We
have also perused the material on record.
5. The incident has occurred in the year 1983 and the Criminal
3

## Page 124

Appeal filed by the appellant herein was of the year 1988 and the
said  appeal  was  disposed  of  by  the  High  Court  only  on
29.05.2026, thirty eight years’ later.
6. All these decades, the appellant herein had the benefit of
bail and it is only pursuant to the disposal of the Criminal Appeal
by the High Court that the appellant has been in jail.
7. Keeping in view the facts and circumstances of the case and
the rival contentions of both sides, we are of the opinion that the
relief in part is made out in this appeal. We, particularly, take
note of the age and ill-health of the appellant herein.
8. Consequently, we allow this appeal in-part by reducing the
sentence of imprisonment imposed by the Trial Court from three
years (including the period already undergone) to ten months and
by increasing the sentence of fine imposed by the Trial Court from
Rs.1,000/- to Rs.10,000/-.
9. The  respondent-State  shall  ascertain  the  period  of
incarceration  of  the  appellant  herein  and  release  him  on
completion of ten months of incarceration on payment of fine
imposed herein in addition to fine already imposed.
4

## Page 125

 
10. This appeal is allowed in part in the aforesaid terms.

2. Heard  learned  Senior  Counsel  on  behalf  of  the
parties.
3. The  controversy  pertains  to  elections  to  the
Panchayat Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies in the
State of Andhra Pradesh. The High Court has, through an
elaborate judgment, dealt with various issues and, in the
penultimate paragraph, has directed the State Election
Commission  to  expeditiously  commence  the  process  of
holding these elections, preferably within six weeks from
the date of judgment, i.e., 01.10.2026. It has been
pointed out that there are State legislations, including
1

## Page 128

the Andhra Pradesh Panchayat Raj Act, 1994 (in short, the
‘1994 Act’), Andhra Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1965, and
Andhra Pradesh Municipal Corporations Act, 1955, to govern
these elections. The High Court, in the final directions,
has expressly held that the electoral roll for the purpose
of these elections shall be in conformity with Section 11
of the 1994 Act.
4. Section 11 of the 1994 Act contemplates that the
electoral roll for Gram Panchayat shall be prepared by the
authorised person in such manner and by reference to such
qualifying  date  as  may  be  prescribed.  The  provision
further says that the electoral roll shall consist of such
part of the electoral roll for the assembly constituencies
published under the Representation of the People Act,
1950, "as revised or amended under the said Act, up to the
qualifying date, as relates to the village or any portion
thereof”. Proviso to Section 11 reads as follows. 
“11. xxx xxx xxx
Provided that any amendment, transposition
or deletion of any entries in the electoral roll,
or any inclusion of names in the electoral roll
of the Assembly Constituencies concerned, made by
the Electoral Registration Officer under section
22 or section 23, as the case may be, of the
Representation of the People Act, 1950, up to the
date of election notification, for any election
held under this Act, shall be carried out in the
electoral roll of the Gram Panchayat and any such
names  included  shall  be  added  to  the  part
relating to the last Ward.”
2

## Page 129

5. As things stand, the Election Commission of India has
issued a Press Note on 30.09.2026, in terms whereof, the
Special Incentive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls in
the State of Andhra Pradesh is proposed to be completed
and the final electoral roll are to be published on
16.10.2026.
6. The State Election Commission has yet not notified
the  election.  Learned  Senior  Counsel  for  the  Andhra
Pradesh State Election Commission states that the election
will be notified within the period granted by the High
Court.
7. That being so, we clarify that if the final electoral
roll prepared by the Election Commission of India upon
completion of the SIR is published before the date of
notification  of  elections  by  the  State  Election
Commission, such revised electoral roll shall be treated
as the final electoral roll for the purpose of conducting
the elections. However, if, for any reason, the final
electoral roll pursuant to the SIR is not published before
the  date  of  notification  of  elections  by  the  State
Election Commission, the elections shall be conducted on
the basis of the previously existing electoral roll, in
accordance with Sections 11 and 12 of the 1994 Act.
3

## Page 130

8. With this clarification, the appeal is disposed of.
9. Pending applications, if any, also stand disposed of.

O R D E R
This is a petition filed under Section 25 of the Code of
Civil Procedure, 1908 (for short “CPC”). The petitioner has
filed this Transfer Petition seeking the following reliefs:
“(a)  Transfer the custody petition being G.W.O.P.No.235 of
2023 titled as “ Mr. S. Muthukumar V. Mrs. N. Janani
Rajalakshmi”, as preferred under Sections 3,7 to 10
and 25 of the Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, pending
before the Court of learned Principal District Judge,
Tiruvallur,  Tamil  Nadu  to  the  Family  Court,
Bangalore, Karnataka; and 
(b) Pass such other or further order or orders as this
Hon’ble Court may deem fit and proper on the facts
and in the circumstances of the case.”
Learned counsel for the respondent submitted that the
respondent has now settled at Bengaluru, Karnataka. 
Having heard learned senior counsel for the petitioner
and learned counsel for the respondent and on perusal of the
material on record, we find that the petitioner has made out a
case for transfer of the aforesaid petition.
In the circumstances, the Transfer Petition is allowed
and the custody petition being G.W.O.P.No.235 of 2023 titled
as “S. Madan(A) Muthukumar vs. N. Janani Rajalakshmi ” pending
1

## Page 140

before  the  Court  of  learned  Principal  District  Judge,
Thiruvallur, Tamil Nadu is ordered to be transferred to the
Family Court, Bengaluru, Karnataka.
 Learned  counsel  for  the  respondent  submitted  that
pursuant to the order dated 20.08.2026, the respondent has
exercised his visitation rights vis-a-vis the minor children
on  the  dates  mentioned  in  the  said  order;  that  pending
disposal of  G.W.O.P. No.235 of 2023 now transferred to the
Principal  Judge,  Family  Court,  Bengaluru,  Karnataka,  an
interim arrangement may be made. 
We have heard learned senior counsel for the petitioner
and learned counsel for the respondent. The earlier order
dated  20.08.2026,  which  is  extracted  as  under,  has  been
complied with:
1.  We  have  heard  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
petitioner and learned counsel for the respondent.
2. Respondent’s counsel submitted that the respondent
has now moved to Bengaluru and settled there. In the
circumstances, a proposal for visitation rights is
being  submitted  to  the  petitioner  for  her
consideration.
3.  Having  heard  learned  senior  counsel  for  the
petitioner and learned counsel for the respondent, we
direct the petitioner to permit the respondent to
exercise  his  visitation  rights  on  29.08.2026,
12.09.2026 and 26.09.2026 from 10:00 A.M. to 3:00 P.M.
depending  upon  the  schedule  of  classes  for  the
children on those days.
4. It is needless to observe that the parties would
cooperate for an effective interaction between the
respondent and the children. In the circumstances, we
have not prescribed any rigid time schedule, it shall
be decided by the parties mutually.
2

## Page 141

5. The respondent shall also be entitled to spend some
time with the daughter on 16.09.2026 which happens to
be her birthday at a mutually convenient timing.
6. Both parties to workout an arrangement of shared
parenting vis-a-vis the children.
7. List on 28.09.2026.”
We  propose  to  make  an  interim  arrangement  pending
disposal of the Guardianship Petition before the Court at
Bengaluru. Consequently, we permit the respondent-father to
have the company of the minor children on alternate second and
fourth Friday evening till second and fourth Sunday evening,
between Friday 8:00 P.M. to Sunday till 5:00 P.M. 
Insofar as the month of the October, 2026 is concerned,
it shall be in third and fifth weekend and from November, 2026
onwards it shall be the second and the fourth weekend.
The respondent shall take all necessary steps to ensure
that the children are comfortable and assist them in all their
activities including home-work and studying for test etc. 
The respondent shall reimburse the petitioner 50% of the
school fees paid by the petitioner to school in which both the
children are studying. 
The petitioner shall also ensure that the respondent
shall exercise his visitation rights in a meaningful manner.
The respondent is also permitted to communicate with the
children  through  video  calls  twice  a  week  on  mutually
convenient days and timings.

1. Heard.

3. Appellant, who has been arraigned as an accused in
P .S. Case No.19/2012 registered for the offences punishable
under Sections 7, 13(2) read with Section 13(1)(d) of the
Prevention  of  Corruption  Act,  1988  is  before  this  Court
seeking for grant of bail and suspension of sentence.
4. The  case  of  the  prosecution  is  that  complainant
Pramod Kumar (PW-2) had alleged that Rudranand Mehta,
Peshkar at the camp office, T orpa had demanded a bribe
1

## Page 145

of  Rs.25,000/-  for  settlement  of  work  relating  to  the
complainant’s land and for the said purpose, a trap was
laid on 30.08.2012 and the bribe amount of Rs.25,000/-
was recovered from the possession of appellant and he
was accordingly arraigned as an accused.
5. Even according to the prosecution, the appellant is
alleged to have received the bribe amount of Rs.25,000/-
from Rudranand Mehta and the said amount was recovered
from the possession of appellant by the trap team. The trial
court has held him guilty of the offence and the appeal is
pending before the High Court. The foundational fact of
demand  and  acceptance  attributable  to  the  appellant
prima facie is an issue which has to be examined by High
Court. The alleged demand was made by Rudranand Mehta
and it was he who had received the amount. In that view of
the matter, we are of the considered view that appellant is
entitled  for  being  released  on  bail  by  suspending  his
sentence imposed by trial court after taking into account
that  he  has  already  spent  one  year  eleven  months
approximately in custody as against the sentence of five
2

## Page 146

years  imposed  on  him.  Hence,  the  appeal  is  allowed,
impugned order is set aside and the sentence imposed on
the appellant stands suspended. Appellant is ordered to be
released  on  bail  on  such  terms  and  conditions  as  the
jurisdictional trial court may deem fit to impose.
6. The  High  Court  without  being  influenced  by  the
observations  made  hereinabove  shall  independently
reassess the evidence and adjudicate the appeal on its own
merits and in accordance with law. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, stands consigned to
records.

O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. Appellants  have  been  arraigned as  accused in  FIR
No.125/2025 for the offences punishable under Sections 8
and 29 of the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances
Act, 1985. On 26.04.2025, police recovered 878 Capsules
of  Dicyclomine  HCl,  Tramadol  HCl  and  Acetaminophen
(Proxyco  SPAS)  weighing  412.66  grams  from  co-accused
Suresh Payala, Mansingh Gurjar and Somdutt Jat. During
1

## Page 155

the course of investigation, it was revealed that appellants,
namely,  Vikram  Saradhana  and  Mahesh  Saradhana
operated  a  medical  store  in  the  name  of  ‘Shiv  Shakti
Medical Store’ and the appellants purchased the capsules
from co-accused Gaurav Khatri and sold them to other co-
accused  by  receiving  payments  sometimes  in  cash  and
sometimes  through  PhonePe.  In  other  words,  the  role
attributed to the appellants is that they operated a medical
store, through which they purchased commercial quantities
of  capsules  of  Dicyclomine  HCl,  T ramadol  HCl  and
Acetaminophen (Proxyco SPAS) from the supplier and sold
the  same  to  the  co-accused,  who  were  subsequently
apprehended with the contraband. Undisputedly, the co-
accused,  namely,  Suresh  Payala,  Mansingh  Gurjar  and
Somdutt  Jat,  who  were  found  in  conscious  physical
possession of the contraband.
4. As  to  whether  appellants  had  indulged  in  sale  of
contraband is an issue which will have to be thrashed out
during  the  course  of  trial  and  it  is  based  only  on  the
statement  of  the  co-accused,  the  appellants  have  been
2

## Page 156

apprehended.  The  appellants  having  no  criminal
antecedents is yet another factor which would sway in our
mind to accept their prayer for grant of bail. Apart from the
fact  that  the  investigation  has  been  completed,
chargesheet has been filed and trial has commenced and
as  such  their  continued  incarceration  is  not  warranted.
Hence, the appeal is allowed, impugned order is set aside
and appellants are ordered to be released on bail on such
terms and conditions as the jurisdictional trial court may
deem fit to impose.
5. Pending application(s), if any, stands consigned to
records.

1. Heard.

3. A sudden inspection conducted on 12.06.2026 by a
joint  team  of  Officers  revealed  shortage  of  2386.52
quintals of paddy and 8554 unused gunny bags, resulting
in alleged financial loss of Rs.77,26,005.01/- to the State.
Consequently,  FIR  bearing  Crime  No.14/2026  was
1

## Page 160

registered against the appellants for criminal breach of
trust and cheating. The role attributed to the appellants
was  they  were  acting  as  the  Manager  of  the  Society
(Contractual)  at  the  Paddy  Procurement  Centre.  They
failed to maintain the stocks properly, committed fraud
and criminal breach of trust. The lack of transparency at
the procurement in charge and the computer operations
thereby  caused  a  substantial  financial  loss  to  the
Government. The prayer for anticipatory bail having been
rejected by both the Courts, they have approached this
Court  and  while  issuing  notice,  interim  protection  was
granted.
4. Ms. Ankita Sharma, learned AOR appearing for the
respondent – State would fairly submit that pursuant to
the  interim  protection  granted,  the  appellants  have
appeared before the Investigating Officer and she would
also hasten to add that further investigation is required to
be made.
5. Having  regard  to  the  fact  that  appellants  have
appeared before the Investigating Officer and the chances
2

## Page 161

of their absconding / flight risk being remote, we are of the
considered view that appellants are entitled for grant of
anticipatory  bail.  Hence,  the  appeals  are  allowed,
impugned orders are set aside and appellants are ordered
to be released on anticipatory bail by the jurisdictional
Investigating Officer on such terms and conditions as he
deems fit to impose including the condition of directing
them to appear before the Investigating Officer on all such
dates as may be notified and on an undertaking given by
the  appellants  that  they  would  appear  before  the  trial
court on all dates of hearing unless specifically exempted.

Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. Though  not  called,  today,  the  respondent
no.2/prosecutrix/complainant is also present in the Court.
3. Learned  counsel  for  the  petitioner  submits  that  the
allegation against the petitioner is of enticing the respondent
no.2 and establishing physical relationship with her after she
got married with another person, which is incorrect for the
reason that the respondent no.2 herself was a willing partner
and in fact, pressurizing the petitioner to marry her and after
the marriage with another person, she on her own volition, had
SLP(Crl.)  No(s).12724/2026

## Page 171

3
left her matrimonial home and thereafter, the allegation that
without being divorced, the petitioner having promised to marry
her, cannot be believed. It was further submitted that the
respondent no.2 herself has taken a stand in a complaint that
she was not happy with the person with whom she was married.
Learned counsel for the petitioner further submitted that the
Court  vide  order  dated  21.07.2026  had  granted  interim
protection to the petitioner during the pendency of the present
petition and pursuant thereto, the petitioner had joined the
investigation  and  thus,  the  Court  may  make  the  interim
protection absolute.
4. Learned counsel for the respondent no.1-State of Madhya
Pradesh submitted that after the above order dated 21.07.2026,
the petitioner has been cooperating with the investigation.
5. Learned counsel for the respondent no.2 submits that there
was specific enticement and the respondent no.2, who in good
faith, believing on the petitioner, has taken the step and now,
she has no place to return as her husband and his family,
cannot be expected to take her back. It was submitted that the
Court would appreciate that no woman would take such step and
SLP(Crl.)  No(s).12724/2026

## Page 172

4
put herself into a situation, where the respondent no.2 is
presently in her life.
6. Having considered the matter, we find that a case for
anticipatory bail has been made out.  As after the interim
protection  was  granted  by  this  Court  vide  order  dated
21.07.2026, we find that the petitioner has presented himself
for the investigation and is cooperating with the investigating
agency, as corroborated by the stand taken by the learned
counsel for the respondent no.1-State of Madhya Pradesh, the
prayer for grant of anticipatory bail is allowed.
7. Accordingly, in the event of arrest or surrender before the
Trial Court by the petitioner within two weeks from today, he
shall be released on bail, subject to such terms and conditions
as may be imposed by the Trial Court and to his cooperation in
the investigating/trial.
8. The Special Leave Petition stands disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
appellants, and the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
respondents. 
3. Respondent No.2 herein had preferred an application under
Section 173(4) of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
(the BNSS) seeking a direction to register an FIR against the
appellant.  The Trial Court dismissed the application.  The
same was reversed by the High Court and a direction was passed
to register an FIR against the appellant. Aggrieved, the
present appeal has been preferred.
4. The issue for consideration is as to whether the High Court is
right in setting aside the order of the Trial Court which
declined to exercise its power under Section 173(4) of the

## Page 195

2
BNSS on the sole premise that in view of the FIR registered at
the instance of the appellant(s) leading to filing of multiple
chargesheets, the subsequent complaint preferred by respondent
No.2 against the appellant will also have to be registered and
thereafter proceeded with. 
5. Neither the High Court has found fault with the reasoning
given by the Trial Court nor any cogent reasoning has been
given  by  them  for  allowing  the  criminal  petition.
Notwithstanding the arguments made on merit, the order cannot
can be sustained in the eye of law on that score alone. Thus,
without going into the submissions made by the learned counsel
appearing for the parties, we are not in a position to give
our  impromptu  to  the  order  passed  by  the  High  Court.
Accordingly, the same stands set aside. 
6. That leaves us to the next issue raised by Mr. Dama Seshadri
Naidu, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondents.
It is submitted by him that the first complaint has been
given, on behalf of the respondent – Mamta Bansal. Admittedly,
she is the wife of the accused in the complaint given by the
appellant(s). We do not wish to say anything on that except by
giving liberty to the respondents to take recourse to law. 
7. With the aforesaid observations, the appeals stand allowed.

away from the police station, yet the police report has been

entitled  to  be  released  on  bail  after  suspension  of

O R D E R 
 
Leave granted. 
2. The appellant is the 4 th accused in a case registered 
under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act,  
19851 and the allegation was that she had received a packet 
from the co-accused; two of whom were apprehended along 
with her , and the packet contained dried leaves  and buds  
with strong odour , which was later identified as marijuana. 
The appellant also was subjected to a medical test , wherein 
she was detected to have used marijuana. The alleged sellers 
of marijuana near the educational institution were 
apprehended with much more quantity of marijuana, which 
 
1 In short ‘NDPS Act’ 

## Page 210

Page 2 of 4 
 
 
was kept in the Scooty on which they came to the spot , from 
where they were apprehended. The c o-accused disclosed  
the names of their supplier, who is also arrayed in the case.  
3. Insofar as the appellant is concerned, even according 
to the statements of the officers of the police team, there was 
no recovery made from her or from the bag which she 
carried. In fact, the specific case is that the Sub-Inspector of 
Police, Nandigama Police Station, received a credible 
information that two persons were coming to sell marijuana 
near a college. The same was intimated to the superior 
officers and deputation of two government employees  were 
sought from the Tahsildar  to act as p anch witness es. The 
police team along with  independent witnesses reached the 
spot at about 02:30 pm. At 03:00 pm, two persons arrived on  
a Scooty and halted at a distance of 100  meters from where 
the police team was carrying out surveillance. The appellant 
is said to have emerged from the college, approached the 
two persons who were standing near the Scooty, who handed 
over a cover to the girl, which was kept in her bag.  
4. The police immediately pounced on the three and the 
allegation is that the appellant produced the cover from her 
bag; voluntarily. In fact , when the police saw the appellant 
putting the cover in the bag, they should have informed her 

## Page 211

Page 3 of 4 
 
 
about her right to be examined before a Magistrate and then 
they should have carried  out the search, if she consents to 
that. The version that the girl produced the cover voluntarily, 
raises a suspicion also with respect to the knowledge of the 
appellant, that there was a contraband in the cover. In fact , 
the entire case set up against the appellant is based on the 
confession, said to have been made by the co -accused; the 
two persons who had commercial quantity of marijuana with 
them and the confession of the appellant herself.  
5. Learned Counsel for the State points out that there was 
apprehension of the appellant from the scene of occurrence, 
and she had voluntarily produced the contraband. It is also 
submitted that the Government, as per the notification 
issued, would not press for a prosecution if the appellant 
agrees to subject herself to a de-addiction process. 
6. Trite is the principle that no confession can be relied 
on. The contraband also having not been recovered from the 
appellant, we are of the opinion that there would be no useful 
purpose served in carrying out a  prosecution against the 
appellant. We are of the opinion that the Police should be 
more sensitive in such matters, especially since the 
appellant, in one way, is a victim being last in the chain of 
supply. Prosecuting such victims can have a spiralling effect 

## Page 212

Page 4 of 4 
 
 
and incarceration pending trial, can lead to more disastrous 
consequences of the victim joining the supply chain, by 
reason only of associations developed in prisons. Curbing 
availability and breaking the supply chain shall be the focus 
and not merely punishing the user, who is actually the victim. 
7. We make it clear that we have not looked at the case 
of the other accused who have been arrayed in S.C. NDPS No. 
91/2025 pending before the Special Sessions Judge, Fast 
Track Court, Rangareddy District, LB Nagar.  
8. Insofar as the appellant is concerned, her arraignment 
in the Sessions Case stands quashed. We are not persuaded 
to subject the appellant to a de-addiction process, especially 
since we find no  complicity insofar as the appellant is 
concerned with respect to the allegations raised of conscious 
possession of narcotics. 
9. The appeal stands allowed. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

1. The  petitioner  before  this  Court  has  filed  the
present Special Leave Petition seeking grant of bail in
connection with FIR No. 19 of 2025, registered at Police
Station Deoband, Saharanpur, Uttar Pradesh. The petitioner
has been in jail for the last 1 year and 8 months. The
facts of the case reveal that the FIR was registered on
18.01.2025 against the petitioner, along with 11 named
persons and about 18 to 20 unnamed persons. A cross-FIR was
also registered in the matter on 19.01.2025 against 22
named persons and about 50 to 55 unknown persons, meaning
thereby that there was a group clash between two groups.
The FIR specifically defines the role of the petitioner.
2. Learned counsel for Respondent No.1, the State of
Uttar Pradesh, has vehemently argued before this Court that
one of the witnesses has turned hostile during the trial
and, therefore, the petitioner should not be released on
bail, as there are three criminal antecedents against the
petitioner. Learned counsel for the complainant has also
argued before this Court that bail should not be granted to
the petitioner, as one of the witnesses has turned hostile.
PETITION(S) FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO(S).  14579/2026

## Page 220

3
3. This Court has carefully gone through the record. In
the present case, there was a group clash between two
groups, and the petitioner has been in jail for the last 1
year and 8 months. It has been brought to the notice of
this Court that two co-accused persons, namely, Tanjim and
Priyanshu Pandit , have already been granted bail. This
Court, after carefully considering the arguments advanced
by the parties and perusing the record, is of the opinion
that the prayer for grant of bail deserves to be allowed
and is accordingly allowed,  subject to furnishing bail
bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to
such other terms and conditions as may be imposed by it.
4. As it has been brought to the notice of this Court
that there is possibility of influencing the witnesses, the
petitioner herein will not enter in Deoband, district
Saharanpur, except for attending trial proceedings in the
aforesaid criminal case.
5.  Needless to observe, the petitioner shall not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat or
promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the facts of
the case from disclosing such facts to the court.
6.   In the event there is any breach of the terms and
conditions for grant of bail, the trail court shall be at
liberty to cancel the bail of the petitioner.
7. It  is  also  ordered  that  the  petitioner  shall
PETITION(S) FOR SPECIAL LEAVE TO APPEAL (CRL.)  NO(S).  14579/2026

diligently attend proceedings of the trial unless exempted.

8. The trial court is requested to conclude the trial at

would preempt the parties from raising all issues in the event
fresh arbitration proceedings are initiated.
3. In that view of the matter, the appeals are allowed, setting
aside the observations made by the learned single Judge as well
as the Division Bench on the merits of the matter.  However,
the finding to the effect that the arbitral award passed by the
learned Arbitrator by re-entering upon the reference is liable
to be set aside is sustained.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.              OF 2026  
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 12498/2026)
SUMAN UTTAMRAO LONDHE      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
RAKESH KAVISHANLAL AGRAWAL & ANR.       RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent(s).
3. Shorn  of  details,  it  appears  that  son  of  the
appellant,  Mahesh  Uttamrao  Londhe,  and  one  Rakesh
Kavishanlal Agrawal had entered into a compromise decree
dated 28.02.2022 in Suit (L) No.2796 of 2022 before the
Original Side of the Bombay High Court (briefly ‘the High
Court’ hereinafter).
4. Appellant  filed  an  interlocutory  application  for
recall of the compromise decree on the ground that it was
in violation of the Will of her late husband and entered
into collusively by the parties to the suit keeping her in
the dark. By the impugned order dated 08.07.2025, the High
Court noted Clause-15 of the Consent Terms as well as the
statement made on behalf of the original plaintiff (Rakesh
Kavishanlal Agrawal) and the original defendant (Mahesh
Uttamrao Londhe) and held that Clause-15 would not be
1

## Page 239

acted upon during the lifetime of the appellant. It may be
mentioned that as per Clause-15 of the Consent Terms,
appellant had to vacate the suit premises in the event of
the  original  defendant,  Mahesh  Uttamrao  Londhe,
predeceasing her.
5. The High Court further observed that there is no bar
in filing a separate suit for asserting the rights of the
appellant traceable to the Will of her late husband,
though it is not permissible for her now to challenge the
compromise decree, being a stranger to the suit.
6. We are of the considered opinion that the view taken
by the High Court warrants no interference. We find
support from a decision of this Court in  Triloki Nath
Singh  versus  Anirudh  Singh  (Dead)  through  Legal
Representatives And Others, [(2020) 6 Supreme Court Cases
629], wherein this Court held that a compromise decree
cannot be assailed by a litigant who was not a party to
the suit by instituting a separate suit. Such a suit would
not be maintainable.
7. Without assailing the compromise decree, appellant is
well within her right to assert her claim based on the
Will by instituting a substantive suit.
8. We have been informant at the Bar that such a suit
has indeed been instituted by the appellant before the
City Civil Court at Mumbai.
9. We, therefore, grant liberty to the appellant to
proceed with the said suit. We make it clear that neither
2

## Page 240

the Consent Terms/Decree nor any observations made by the
High Court would come in the way in the adjudication of
the suit which shall be decided on its own merit. In the
meanwhile, paragraph No.11 of the impugned order dated
08.07.2025 passed by the High Court would continue to
operate till disposal of the suit.
10. The Civil Appeal is disposed of.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

6. By  way  of  the  present  appeal,  the  appellant
challenges the order dated 25.01.2024 in Criminal Appeal
No.185/2007 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at
Indore.
7. On going through the impugned order, we find that the
submission of learned counsel for the appellant before
the High Court was that he had no instructions as the
whereabouts of the appellant were not known. Bailable
warrants having been issued against the appellant, the
same  were  not  executed.  The  High  Court,  instead  of

## Page 247

waiting for the execution of the warrant, on its own
proceeded to decide the appeal in the absence of the
appellant, without appointing an Amicus Curiae or a legal
aid counsel to project the case of the appellant. Even on
merits, nothing has been discussed with regard to the
specific assertions, statements of witnesses, etc. The
impugned  order  is  sketchy  and,  it  being  a  criminal
appeal, was not expected to be decided in such a casual
manner, specially when it was his first appeal against
the order of conviction and sentence.
8. In light of the above, we set aside the impugned
order dated 25.01.2024 and remand the case back to the
High Court for a fresh decision in accordance with law.

Principal Judge, Family Court, Faridabad, Haryana to the
Principal  Judge,  Family  Court,  North-East  District,

refusing to accept the closure report, passed the following
operative order:-
“XXXX
The  request  made  by  the  Superintendent  of  Police
(City), Surajpur, vide Article A-13, which pertains to
the closure of this case, is, therefore, on the basis
of the above facts, not fit to be accepted and is
hereby disallowed. Let the final report, together with
the pages of the case diary, be paginated and sent
back  to  the  police  station  concerned,  with
acknowledgment taken, for taking further appropriate
action in the case; and let copies of the documents
annexed  to  the  chargesheet  (challan),  which  stand
marked as exhibits in this closure case, be annexed to
this closure case.
Let  a  copy  of  the  order  be  sent  to  the  Senior
Superintendent of Police, Surajpur, and to the Officer
In-charge, Police Station Jainagar, for taking further
appropriate action.”
4. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner(s) submits that
the Court could not direct filing of the charge-sheet.
5. We accept the contention of the learned Senior Counsel
and delete the direction with regard to submission of the
charge-sheet.”
6. We noticed from the impugned order that interim order

## Page 283

3
passed, has been vacated.
7. The consequence of our above direction would be that the
order dated 14.10.2025 of the aforesaid Trial Court will
continue to operate and the Investigating Authorities will take
such steps as are required in law, in accordance with the said
direction.
8. Learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner(s) submits that
the petitioner is entitled to have the petition for quash heard
on merits.
9. However,  there  shall  be  no  interim  order  for  the
petitioner.
10. Since the matter is to be listed on 15.10.2026, we
request the High Court to make an endevour to hear the  matter
on that date or on such earlier date as may deem fit.
11. With these observations, the Special Leave Petition is
disposed of.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed
of.

## Page 333

We are not inclined to interfere with the
findings of the courts below declining to grant a
decree of specific performance.  However, the Trial
Court directed refund of the advance amount of  10₹
lakhs with interest at the rate of 6% per annum,
which order has been affirmed  by the High Court.
According to the respondent’s counsel an amount of
17,46,500/- was deposited on 7₹ th September, 2026 with
the Trial Court.
Considering the facts and circumstances of the
case,  we  are  of  the  view  that  the  plaintiff-
petitioner, who has been deprived of the amount of
10  lakhs  by  the  defendant(s)-respondent(s)  for₹
almost  13  years,  deserves   to  be  suitably
compensated.  We feel that a total amount of   40₹
lakhs would  be a  reasonable and  fair amount  to
compensate the petitioner. 
Accordingly, we direct that the  plaintiff-
petitioner  shall be entitled to receive a total
amount  of   40  lakhs  from  the  defendant(s)-₹
respondent(s). Since an amount of   17,46,500/- is₹
already lying in deposit with the Trial Court, we
direct the  respondent(s) to pay the balance amount
of   22,53,500/- within a period of two months from₹
today. 
The said amount may be deposited with the

deposit, the Trial Court shall release the   said

along with accrued interest, if any,  shall also be
released within the next two weeks from today to the
plaintiff-petitioner   upon   his  furnishing  the
necessary bank details.
With the abovesaid observations the special
leave petition stands disposed of. Impugned order(s)

IA No. 302185/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.

CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE MANOJ MISRA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DEVENDRA KUMAR UPADHYAYA
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Nidesh Gupta, Sr. Adv.

For Respondent(s) : 
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The case of the petitioners is that appointments are governed
by 2018 Service Rules which defines ‘Government’ as follows:
“Government means the Government of the
State  of  Punjab,  in  the  Department  of
School Education”
2.  The unamended 2018 Service Rules specified the eligibility
criteria, inter alia, providing that a candidate must be possessed
of requisite teaching experience of three years in any Government
1

## Page 393

school. This eligibility criterion was amended  vide notification
dated 13.02.2020 to read as under:
“Should possess teaching experience for a
minimum period of three years on the post
of a teacher in any Government school under
the control of the Director.”
3. At  this  stage,  recruitment  advertisements  were  issued.
Admittedly, the recruitment notices i.e. advertisements were in
conformity with the extant Rules. However, certain candidates
questioned the 2020 amendment even though it did not make any
material  difference  as  the  definition  of  Government  was  not
amended. Therefore, there was no stay on recruitment exercise,
which continued, though the declaration of results was put on hold.
4. In between, the aforesaid eligibility criterion was further
amended vide notification dated 12.09.2025 to read as under:
“Should possess teaching experience for
a minimum period of seven years on the
post  of  teacher  working  on  regular
basis in any Government School.”
5. According to the petitioners, based upon the amendment, which
was prospective, without any rational basis, the State took a
decision to withdraw the recruitment notification. This decision of
withdrawal was questioned by the petitioners before the High Court
by contending that there was no merit in the challenge to the 2020
amendment,  therefore,  the  advertisements,  whereunder  the
recruitment exercise had proceeded substantially, did not merit
withdrawal. However, by the impugned order the writ petitions were
dismissed. 
6. The submission is that the petitioners have been arbitrarily
2

## Page 394

deprived of their right to be considered for appointment under a
lawful advertisement against existing posts in terms of the extant
service rules.
7. Issue notice on the special leave petitions as well as interim
application, returnable on 16.11.2026.
           
(CHETAN ARORA)                                  (SAPNA BANSAL)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        COURT MASTER (NSH)
3
